Solving a research problem is like solving a detective mystery. The task requires planning and
the careful collection of facts. With a little planning, your research experience can be posi-
tive and rewarding. This unit illustrates two additional types of research tools. Chapters 46
and 47 deal with the topic of simulation and Chapter 48 provides an outline for performing
a Market Basket Analysis with the aid of clustering methods.
Simulation typically is nothing more or less than the technique of performing sampling
experiments on the model of the system. The experiments are done on the model rather than
on the real system itself only because the latter would be too inconvenient, expensive, and
time consuming. Otherwise, simulated experiments should be viewed as virtually indistin-
guishable from ordinary statistical experiments, so that they also should be based upon sound
statistical theory. Simulated experiments usually are executed on a computer because of the
vast amount of data being generated and processed rather than because of any inherent rela-
tionship between the experiment and the computer.
Tartakovsky’s article as well as the research study vignette presented in Chapter 48 illustrate
the breadth of topics and methods in the realm of computing research methods. A short list of
computing research methods includes: field studies, instrument /product development, soft-
ware experiments, mathematical proofs, simulation, model building, and conceptual analysis.
Information systems focus is on:
n developing an understanding of the process of developing and using information and
communication technologies in an organization, and
n filling the gap between the foci of attention by the fields of engineering and the
behavioral sciences/economics.
The focus of engineering is upon producing new technological capabilities, while the behav-
ioral sciences /economics focus is to recommend trends on the basis of technological capacity.
In summary, information systems has:
n developed knowledge to explain socio-economic changes associated with information
technologies, and
n provided associated relevant guidance to the organizations for necessary action.
Therefore the information system researcher employs a variety of research methods and
pursues a variety of theoretical perspectives.

chunks.heading: 46.1 Introduction
chunks.content:
46.1 Introduction
The methodology of simulation, initially used by operations research, was created by John
von Neumann and Stanislaw Ulam in the late 1940s. Since the advent of digital computing,
simulation has been used for countless business applications. Essentially, simulation is the
use of a system model that has the desired characteristics of reality in order to reproduce
the essence of the actual operations. The Monte Carlo method is simulation by sampling
techniques. It involves determining the probability distribution of the variable under con-
sideration and then sampling from this distribution by means of random numbers to obtain
data. In effect, a set of random numbers is used to generate a set of values that have the same
distributional characteristics as the actual experience it is desired to simulate. In this chapter,
we will study Monte Carlo simulation with actual business applications.

The bulletins sell for $4.00, and the variable cost of producing each bulletin is $1.50. Left-

which we compute the revenue where:
Revenue = MIN(produced, demand) * unit-price.
Additionally, we need to compute the total production cost where:
Total production cost = produced * unit-prod-cost.

1. The use of games and simulations raises many questions about their use, the role of
the teacher, the time and space required, which games are appropriate, evaluation
procedures, and the benefits and drawbacks of using games. Little research is
available on evaluating games and simulations and how teachers can be assisted in

b. Present an outline of how to evaluate and design games and simulations in the
populations of business, finance, and economics.

Chapter 46 presented a brief overview of the Monte Carlo Method. This technique is a
computational technique applied to static models. Static models provide for the relationship
between the system attributes when the system is in equilibrium. If a point of equilibrium
is changed by altering any of the attribute values, then the model enables the new values for
all the attributes to be derived. However, the model does not show ‘how’ the attribute values
were modified.
Dynamic models follow the changes over time that result from the system attributes. In
this chapter, an algorithm for a discrete event simulation is presented through applying the
dynamic model which maintains a current events chain. A polling and reassignment of attri-
bute values take place each time an event experiences a change of state.

47.3 d iscrete e vent s imulation
The previous examples of simulation we discussed did not involve time as an element of the
simulation. Such simulations are referred to as static. However, many systems experience
changes in state over time. For example, inventory and queuing systems have the state vari-
ables change only at a discrete set of points in time and are called discrete event simulations.
But consider the water behind a dam. Clearly evaporation and heavy rains make the state
variable. The water level experiences changes in state continuously over time. Systems like
this are referred to as continuous simulations.
Consider simulating a network system. For this type of study, the researcher must:
n Identify the system, which is a collection of entities that interact over time to
accomplish the goals of the study.
n Construct a model, or an abstract representation of the system that describes a
system in terms of state, entities and related attributes, sets, events, activities, and
delays.
c The system state is a collection of variables that contain all of the information to
describe the system at any time.
c A set is simply a collection of associated states.
c An event is an occurrence that changes the state of a system.
c A known time interval, such as for servicing an entity, is an activity.
c A time interval of unknown length until an activity is actually completed, such as a
wait time in a queue, is referred to as a delay.
When setting up a discrete event simulation, one must operationally define the system state,
